catalog_quote: [p.127, sec. 5.6:] For V2 vowels, no correspondences exist because it is not possible to reconstruct the quality of that vowel for virtually every root. From the PB roots and PM tones, it is clear that a second vowel must have been present in noun stems. Many of these vowels have been lost before and others since PM (cf. also 3.3.4 and end of 6.4.2). This may be described as a general trend which has been taking place over a long period of time. There appears to be no specific cause for this loss but it could possibly have to do with stress on the stem initial syllable. However, since tone is the main suprasegmental phenomenon which has distinctive function, stress is not often discussed and therefore the relationship of tone and stress is not well understood. ... new_statements.rule_in_words: The Manenguba languages (including the Bassossi varieties NSW and MYE) are tone languages with two phonological tones, H and L (plus downstep and HL/LH contours); the author does not describe word stress synchronically and only speculates, at the level of the whole group / Proto-Manenguba, that the historical loss of stem-final vowels might be due to stress on the stem-initial syllable, adding that stress in these languages is little discussed and its relation to tone not understood.
new_statements.exceptions: None; the remark is explicitly hedged ('could possibly') and comparative, not a rule with exceptions.
new_statements.domain_note: Diachronic/comparative remark about noun (and verb) stems across all 14 Manenguba varieties; 'stem initial syllable' = root-initial syllable (prefixes excluded). No statement about the phonological word, phrase level, or citation forms in Bassossi specifically.
new_statements.identity_note: Glottolog bass1260 / ISO bsi 'Bassossi' corresponds to two of Hedinger's 14 Manenguba varieties: NSW (nswase, Basossi; informant Max Akpo Anang) and MYE (Mienge, Mbo of Nguti); Glottolog's own language code mapping of Hedinger 1987 assigns MYE to [bsi], and Ethnologue/OLAC list Mienge, Nswase, Nsose, Lower Mbo as names of bsi. Hedinger (1984:271-272) groups MYE-NSW as the 'North Western group' (93%/84% cognate), distinct from Akoose [bss, akoo1248] and Bakaka [bqz, baka1273]. The quoted stress remark is NOT variety-specific: it is a hedged, diachronic aside about the Manenguba group / Proto-Manenguba as a whole.

sources.note: Comparative-historical study of 14 Manenguba varieties incl. NSW (Nswase/Basossi) and MYE (Mienge). Sec. 2.5 Tone (p.47): phonologically only H and L tones, downdrift, downstep, HL/LH contours. Only stress remark, sec. 5.6 p.127 (PDF p.128): loss of stem V2 'could possibly have to do with stress on the stem initial syllable. However, since tone is the main suprasegmental phenomenon which has distinctive function, stress is not often discussed'. Group-level, hedged; nothing specific to Bassossi.
